overview.body: This is a BUILD unit! You'll copy your Lab 1.3 code and turn the one-roll game into a real trip: roll after roll until you arrive. Along the way your menu learns to refuse bad choices, Galveston comes back inside a second loop, and your report learns to count.

mentorQuote.quote: Module 1 was one roll and done. Real trips don't work that way, and neither does real software: most programs are a loop that keeps going until something says stop. Once you can write that loop, the game finally feels like a game.

objectives: Start from your finished Lab 1.3 and delete what a loop replaces, line by line
Refuse bad menu choices with an input validation loop
Travel turn by turn with a while loop and a counter
Keep going to Galveston with a nested loop: one pass of the outer loop per leg
Add up the trip with accumulators and print the STATISTICS block
Test every path, including bad choices and big last rolls
overview.keyConceptsText: Chapter 4 Sections: 4.1 (Repetition Structures), 4.2 (The while Loop), 4.4 (Calculating a Running Total), 4.6 (Input Validation Loops), 4.7 (Nested Loops)
overview.textbookReference: Starting Out with Python, 6th Edition by Tony Gaddis, Chapter 4: Repetition Structures

Your program MUST print the STATISTICS block in the Final Trip Report

content.body: Right now a 5 at the menu means the trip never starts. A while loop fixes that: it keeps asking until the player types 1, 2, or 3.

A while loop repeats its block as long as its condition is true. Here the condition is "the choice is out of range," so the block runs only when the answer is bad, and the loop stops the moment the answer is good. This is called an input validation loop. Every choice that gets past it is 1, 2, or 3, so the chain's last branch can be a plain else, and the invalid-choice message has nothing left to do.

content.body: The heart of Module 2. Instead of one roll deciding everything, you roll turn after turn until you arrive. Every trip makes it now; the only question is how many turns it takes.

The loop keeps going while miles_remaining is more than zero. Each turn subtracts that turn's miles, so the condition eventually turns false and the loop stops. leg_turns is a counter: it starts at 0 and goes up by 1 at the start of each turn. The roll prompt from Module 1 moves inside the loop; in Lab 2.2, Python rolls for you, and that's the line that changes.

content.quote: Read a while loop from the bottom of the body back to the top. What changes each time through? miles_remaining. Does that change move it toward the condition being false? Every roll is at least 1, so yes. If you can answer those two questions, your loop ends.

content.body: Galveston is back. Make it to Houston, and the game asks whether you want to keep going, the same question as Lab 1.3. Say yes, and the travel loop runs again for the last 50 miles.

A loop inside another loop is a nested loop. The loop you wrote in CP3 drives one leg, turn by turn. The new outer loop runs once per leg, and after each leg it decides whether there's another one. That decision is a Boolean variable, like Lab 1.3's reached_beach: playing starts each pass as False, and only a yes in Houston sets it back to True.

content.quote: The inner loop drives one leg. The outer loop decides whether there's another leg. Keep those two jobs straight and a nested loop is just two loops you already understand, one inside the other. When I'm not sure which loop a line belongs to, I look at its indentation before I look at anything else.

content.code:
# Travel one leg at a time
    playing = True
    while playing:
        # Travel turn by turn until you arrive
        print('=' * 50)
        print(f'TRAVELING TO {destination.upper()}!')
        print('=' * 50)
        print()

        miles_remaining = distance
        leg_turns = 0
        while miles_remaining > 0:
            leg_turns = leg_turns + 1
            print(f'--- Turn {leg_turns} ---')
            print(f'Miles remaining: {miles_remaining}')
            roll = int(input('Enter your roll (1-20): '))
            miles_this_turn = roll * MILES_MULTIPLIER
            print(f'You rolled a {roll}!')
            print(f'You travel {miles_this_turn} miles...')
            miles_remaining = miles_remaining - miles_this_turn
            if miles_remaining <= 0:
                print()
                print(f'You made it to {destination}!')
            else:
                print(f'Miles remaining: {miles_remaining}')
            print()
        current_city = destination

        # Keep going to Galveston?
        playing = False
        if current_city == 'Houston':
            answer = input('Continue to Galveston? (y/n): ')

                distance = HOU_TO_GALVESTON
                print(f"You're headed to {destination}!")
                print(f'Distance: {distance} miles')

content.body: The report gets its first new section: STATISTICS, with the trip's total miles and turns, across every leg. It's the same block your game prints all semester; Lab 2.2 adds hazard lines to it.

An accumulator is a variable that starts at 0 and has something added to it again and again. total_miles adds each turn's miles inside the inner loop. total_turns adds each leg's turns, once per pass of the outer loop. Both start before either loop, so a trip to Galveston counts both legs: leg_turns starts over for the second leg, and the totals don't.
